title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) False Start
summary: This informational RFC specifies an optional TLS client behavior called False Start. It affects only timing, not the on-the-wire data, can be implemented unilaterally, and reduces handshake latency to one round trip.

plainLanguage.summary: TLS False Start lets a client send application data before it has received the server's handshake confirmation. This can save a round trip, but only under specified security conditions.

questions: how to reduce tls handshake latency
how does false start reduce tls latency
subtitle: A TLS client behavior that can send application data one round trip sooner

tldr.problem: A full TLS handshake through TLS 1.2 requires two protocol rounds before application data can flow, adding latency when the client sends first.
tldr.mechanism: If the application requests it and approved ciphers, protocol versions, key exchanges, and client certificate types are used, the client may send application data after its Finished message but before receiving the server's Finished.
tldr.outcome: False Start reduces the handshake latency for client-first applications to one round trip, with security restrictions because the server has not yet been authenticated.

today: RFC 7918 is an Informational document and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text says False Start is not needed with TLS 1.3 and later, which are outside its scope.

sections.title: Reducing the TLS Handshake Delay
sections.content:
A full handshake in TLS versions up to TLS 1.2 requires two protocol rounds before application data can be sent. For applications where the client speaks first, such as HTTP, that can add two network round-trip times.

With False Start, the client may send application data after its own ChangeCipherSpec and Finished messages, before it has received the server's corresponding messages. If the handshake completes, the transcript differs only in timing. If it fails, data has already been sent before the handshake was validated.
sections.plainLanguage: False Start lets a client send data before the full handshake finishes. This saves time, but the client does not yet know whether the handshake will be validated.

sections.title: Server Compatibility
sections.content:
False Start is optional. A server is False Start compatible if it tolerates receiving TLS records before it is ready to process them. A client can successfully use False Start only when the server has this behavior.

The RFC says this requirement generally does not hinder deployment. Typical implementations can be compatible without special False Start support because the transport layer buffers early records until the server is ready.
sections.plainLanguage: The server must tolerate receiving application records early. Transport buffering often lets an implementation do this without special False Start logic.

sections.title: When a Client May Start Early
sections.content:
A client MAY send application data early only when the application requested False Start and each negotiated element is on the relevant whitelist: the symmetric cipher, protocol version, key exchange method and parameters, and, when client authentication is used, the client certificate type.

The rules for receiving data do not change. Sending data does not mean the server is authenticated. The RFC recommends allowing the application to ask whether the handshake has completed.
sections.plainLanguage: The client may start early only if the application asks and every negotiated security choice passes the required checks. The application must not treat early send permission as proof that the server is authenticated.

sections.title: Why False Start Has Security Limits
sections.content:
TLS Finished messages validate the handshake, including the negotiated cipher suite and key exchange. False Start sends data before that validation, so an attacker may have altered the handshake and the client cannot yet be sure it is communicating with the expected peer.

The RFC's security goal is that anyone able to decrypt early data must be the legitimate peer. It recommends strong symmetric ciphers, whitelisting the protocol version, and key exchanges and parameters that provide forward secrecy. For the recommendations in the RFC, the key length is generally at least 128 bits, DH groups at least 3,072 bits, and named curves at least 256 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Before Finished messages are checked, the client cannot confirm the peer's identity. False Start therefore permits early data only with approved cryptographic choices.

sections.title: Abbreviated Handshakes and Later TLS Versions
sections.content:
An abbreviated handshake used to resume an earlier TLS session already takes one round trip before client-first application data can begin, so the RFC says client-side False Start is not needed for that case. The document does not further consider server-side False Start.

TLS 1.3 and later are outside the scope of RFC 7918. The RFC says False Start will not be needed with those versions because reducing the number of round trips is a design goal.
sections.plainLanguage: Session resumption already reduces the delay for client-first traffic. RFC 7918 covers versions through TLS 1.2 and says False Start is not needed for TLS 1.3 and later.
